participation.text: Many signings, refusals and absent opportunities complicate any claim of uniform consent.

evidence.text: Two language versions require comparison in context.

name: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: texts, signatures and authority
place: Waitangi and signing places across Aotearoa New Zealand
geographicPrecision: Initial signing locator; sheets circulated to other places and did not reach every community.

interval.label: Initial signing 6 February 1840; further signings through 1840
interval.note: Document/signing chronology, not the beginning or end of Māori identity or agreement on every later interpretation.

question: What happens when two texts promise different things?
summary: Rangatira debated words, sought assurances and made different decisions as Treaty sheets circulated. The Māori text, the original English text and later translations need separate labels. Promises of authority and protection must also be tested against subsequent Crown actions.

sections.title: An agreement took work
sections.text: Te Tiriti was made through drafting, translation, speeches, questions and marks. Henry Williams and his son Edward translated an English draft into Māori before the Waitangi hui. Rangatira discussed land and the authority of the proposed governor, rather than merely witnessing a ceremony. Those who signed on 6 February 1840 signed or marked the Māori text. Missionaries and officials then carried copies elsewhere. Reading the documents matters, but so do the explanations and assurances through which people encountered them.

sections.title: Keep three kinds of text distinct
sections.text: The original English article 1 claims a transfer of sovereignty. The Māori article uses kāwanatanga; article 2 guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga. In his later scholarly translation, Hugh Kawharu renders the first term as government and the retained authority as chieftainship. His English translation is not the English document of 1840. Comparing articles 1 and 2 together raises a practical question: who would make decisions, and what authority and resources would communities retain?

citations.locator: Original Māori/English articles 1–2; separate Kawharu translation

sections.title: Sheets record different decisions
sections.text: The surviving set contains nine sheets, including one English sheet and a printed Māori sheet. Colenso’s printing helped circulate the wording; the surviving printed sheet’s signing dates are unknown. Making copies expanded the document’s reach while leaving different local discussions to be reconstructed. Some Waikato rangatira signed the English sheet; Te Wherowhero declined. At Ōnuku, in the Ngāi Tahu takiwā, the Māori Herald-Bunbury sheet was signed on 30 May. Elsewhere, Ngāti Toa rangatira Nohorua wanted his son-in-law to witness his signature because of what future land loss might mean for their descendants. Such decisions concerned relationships and accountability. An identifying mark cannot by itself tell us every assurance heard, every person represented or every expectation held.

sections.title: A claim of power is not its fulfilment
sections.text: Hobson proclaimed British sovereignty on 21 May, before circulation ended. That announcement asserted authority; it did not turn non-signing communities into consenting signatories. Nor did signing ensure that protection would follow. In its 2014 Te Raki findings, the Tribunal concluded that the northern rangatira signing in February had not ceded sovereignty. Its later inquiry described serious Crown breaches during the Northern War, including military attacks on settlements. These findings have named districts and historical scopes. They invite examination of what people were promised and what government subsequently did.

citations.locator: Northern War findings in official release

claims.text: The Māori and English texts differ significantly over governance, sovereignty and retained authority.
claims.checkedBy: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval

returnPrompt: What would you ask before saying that everyone understood an agreement in the same way?

deeperReading.title: Translation remains an attributed interpretation
deeperReading.text: The complete published Māori transcription, English text and Kawharu translation are available through the sources. The capsules here select articles 1 and 2; they do not reproduce the whole agreement. Article 3 also needs attention: Kawharu’s commentary examines tikanga and cautions against assuming that British citizenship language carried identical meanings in both languages. The 2014 Tribunal considered spoken explanations as well as text. Its conclusion concerned February signings in the Bay of Islands and Hokianga, not every signing throughout the country or a ruling on the Crown’s present sovereignty. A later institutional translation helps a reader compare; it cannot stand in for the voice of each rangatira.

citations.locator: All three articles and modern translation

deeperReading.title: Place and speaker change the question
deeperReading.text: Ōnuku Rūnanga describes the signing place as a continuing home and a place for Ngāi Tahu discussion. In a 2025 commemorative speech there, Justin Tipa connected the signatories Iwikau and Tīkao with descendants caring for that gathering. He distinguished collective rangatiratanga from individual citizenship rights and described Ngāi Tahu’s position within a constitutional monarchy. This is a named, dated Ngāi Tahu perspective, not the single Māori answer to every constitutional question. Read alongside the geographically bounded Te Raki inquiry, it shows why evidence needs a place, an audience and a date. Neither source supplies permission to speak for every iwi or hapū.

citations.locator: Ōnuku memory; collective rights and constitutional position

evidenceReading.title: Original wording, recorded marks and a later finding
evidenceReading.introduction: The passages below are selected terms and editorial paraphrases. Original document, published transcription, modern translation and later historical finding remain distinct.

items.label: Two originals and a later translation
items.text: The Māori transcription’s article 1 includes “te Kawanatanga katoa”; article 2 includes “te tino rangatiratanga”. The original English article 1 speaks of sovereignty. Kawharu’s separately labelled translation uses government for the first term.
items.interpretation: Compare the powers being discussed and the guarantees being retained. A translation is an interpretation with an author; it is not a newly discovered original English promise. Māori terms in running explanation use modern macrons; the short quoted transcription retains the source’s spelling.

items.label: A number beside a name
items.text: NZHistory explains that the 1877 facsimiles number signatories for reference. Those numbers need not match signing order, and some identities and affiliations depend on later research.
items.interpretation: A mark, catalogue number and later biographical identification are different evidence. Avoid turning an uncertain name or a blank region on a signing map into proof of agreement or refusal.

items.label: A proclamation and a bounded inquiry
items.text: The 21 May proclamation announces Crown sovereignty. The Tribunal’s 2014 release reaches a different conclusion about what the February northern signatories had agreed to transfer.
items.interpretation: The first records a claim made by the Crown; the second is a later inquiry into the agreement’s meaning in a specified region and month. Neither is a tally of every community’s consent, and neither alone shows how authority was enforced.

familyActivity.title: Label the kind of evidence
steps: Read three supplied capsules: A—the 1840 English article 1 claims sovereignty. B—the Māori text uses kāwanatanga, translated by Kawharu as government, and article 2 guarantees tino rangatiratanga. C—Hobson’s 21 May proclamation asserts Crown sovereignty while signing continued.
Label the original text, the later translation inside a capsule, and the later proclamation. Underline a claim about governing and circle a promise about retained authority.

Ask two questions before calling this universal agreement: which community and occasion are we discussing, and what evidence would show that its promises were carried out? Use the supplied Ōnuku/Te Wherowhero examples to explain why one answer cannot fit every place.
familyActivity.explanation: A and the Māori wording in B are two 1840 texts; Kawharu’s English wording inside B is later interpretation. C is a Crown assertion, not another community’s signature. A promise and its fulfilment require different evidence. The examples show both signing and refusal without assigning either position to all Māori.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author checking; not independent Māori-language, historian, iwi or hapū approval
review.scope: Complete published transcriptions were read; learner capsules select articles 1–2 and a later proclamation. Source-qualified early enforcement and named modern Māori perspectives deepen the unchanged 1840 case. Original identity, complete interval/note/precision, claims, dimensions, coordinates and empty object list remain preserved.
limitations: No independent Māori translation, complete palaeography of the nine sheets, full original voyage journals or all signatory identities checked. Published transcriptions, later statutory editions and modern back-translations are labelled separately.

Kawharu bibliographic attributions differ: Archives labels 1975; Te Papa cites a 1988 report; the current Tribunal page combines 1989 with a later title/editor set. No original composition/publication date for the translation is inferred. The underlying books/reports were not read to resolve that discrepancy.

Waimate’s day and initial signature counts differ among institutional sources. The English sheet’s first signing date is unknown; a witness date is not substituted. The geography is a sourced place/date table, not surveyed coordinates, a complete itinerary, iwi borders or evidence that every region was reached.

Tribunal sources here are official 2014/2022 summaries, not the complete evidentiary reports. Their district, month and historical limits are retained. No current legal claim, contemporary political bill status or completed redress is adjudicated or updated.

The 2025 Tipa speech is a named Ngāi Tahu political perspective; its video and underlying legal references were not independently checked. It does not supply universal Māori assent or approval of this account.

No current media exist for this case. Official Flickr sheet metadata were researched but pixels were not inspected or adopted; item-specific noncommercial/no-derivatives and no-overlay guidance prevents treating a generic website licence as unrestricted image permission.
